title: Nanotechnology in Medicine (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand how very small materials are used in medicine, from imaging to drug delivery, and how safety, testing and ethics apply. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what nanoscale means and give three medical uses.
Use size comparisons and units correctly.
Compare benefits and risks of nanomedicines.
Judge claims in news and adverts.
task: Write a two-page briefing on three medical uses of nanotechnology, with benefits, risks, evidence stage and ethical questions.
condition: A computer, public information, two peers and a mentor. No laboratory work is done in this course.
standard: Units and sizes are correct; each use has an evidence stage; risks are stated; no overclaims; sources dated; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Science students, biomedical trainees, health writers, regulators' assistants.
modules: The nanoscale
Understand
A nanometre is one billionth of a metre. At this size, materials can behave differently from the same material at ordinary size.
1 metre = 1,000,000,000 nanometres. A human hair is about 80,000 nm wide, a red blood cell about 7,000 nm, a virus about 100 nm, a DNA strand about 2 nm.
Small particles have a large surface compared with their volume, so they react faster and interact with cells differently.
Gold particles look red or purple in liquid, not yellow, because of how light interacts with them.
Nano does not mean magic; it means a size range with new properties to test and control.
A gold nanoparticle 20 nm wide is about 4,000 times narrower than a hair. A rapid test strip uses such particles to show a coloured line when a marker is present.
Make a size chart from a metre to an atom with at least eight objects and their sizes in nanometres.
All sizes are within the correct order of magnitude and the chart is labelled with units.
Imaging and diagnostics
Understand
Nanoparticles can make signals clearer or detect small amounts of a marker in a sample.
Contrast agents improve scan images in some tests.
Test strips use nanoparticles to make a line visible, and sensors can detect very small amounts of a substance.
False positives and false negatives still occur, so results must be confirmed when they matter.
Always follow instructions and storage conditions of a test.
A pregnancy test strip uses coloured nanoparticles attached to antibodies. They gather at the test line only if the hormone is present, giving a visible line.
Explain a test strip to a peer in your own words using a drawing.
Peer can repeat how the line forms and one limit of the test.
Drug delivery
Understand
Carriers can protect a drug and help it reach where it is needed.
Lipid (fat-based) particles protect fragile genetic medicines during delivery.
Targeting aims to put drug where it is needed and reduce side effects elsewhere.
Particles can be cleared by the liver and kidneys or trigger immune reactions.
Each carrier is tested for size, stability, safety and release.
Some vaccines use fat-based particles around genetic instructions so that they survive until they reach cells, then release their cargo.
Draw a delivery diagram labelling carrier, drug, target and clearance route.
Diagram labels all four and has no false claims.
Particles in the body
Analyse
Size, shape and surface decide where particles go and how long they stay.
Very small particles may pass through kidneys; larger ones are caught by the liver and spleen.
Surface coatings change how the immune system sees them.
Long-term build-up is a concern for some materials.
Animal-free and human-cell methods help early safety testing where possible.
Studies often report particles around 100 nm circulating longer than particles of 500 nm, which are filtered quickly.
Make a table of size, likely route and a concern for three particle types.
Entries agree with the sources you cite.
Testing and regulation
Evaluate
Nanomedicines go through extra checks because size and surface strongly affect behaviour.
Path: lab studies, safety testing, human trials, regulator review, approval, monitoring after sale.
Regulators ask for particle size distribution, stability, purity and batch consistency.
Manufacturing changes can change behaviour, so they are controlled.
Report side effects to the national system.
A batch is rejected because particle size varied beyond the allowed range. The factory fixes mixing time and re-tests before release.
Map the path from lab to patient with at least six stages and one check at each.
All stages present; checks are specific.
Risks and unknowns
Evaluate
An honest briefing lists uncertainty as clearly as benefit.
Possible concerns: inflammation, accumulation, allergy, effects over many years.
Environmental release during making and disposal needs control.
Workers handling powders need closed systems and protective equipment.
State what is not yet known.
A plant uses closed handling and extraction, masks for sampling, and a waste route for nano-containing material.
List five risks, a control for each and one unknown.
Each risk has a control and the unknown is stated honestly.
Hype, claims and headlines
Analyse
News often reports lab results as if they were cures.
Stage check: idea, lab, animal-free or animal study, human trial, approved.
Be wary of "miracle" words and of results in a single small study.
Look for independent reviews and trial registry entries.
Ask who funded the work.
A headline says tiny particles "destroy cancer". The study is in cells in a dish. The learner labels it "lab stage, not a treatment".
Review three real headlines and assign each an evidence stage.
Each stage is justified with a quote.
Write the balanced briefing
Create
Combine facts, benefits, risks and fairness.
Cover three uses with benefits, risks and stage.
Add access and cost questions.
State what is unknown.
Test with a non-expert.
The reader can explain why approval takes years and why one lab result is not enough.
Write and present a two-page briefing.
Reader repeats three limits correctly.
quiz: How many nanometres in a metre?
1,000,000,000. (Covered in module 1: The nanoscale. To pass that module: Orders of magnitude correct.)
Name a medical use.
Imaging, test strips or drug delivery. (Covered in module 2: Imaging and diagnostics. To pass that module: Peer understands.)
Why does size matter in the body?
It decides where particles go and how they clear. (Covered in module 3: Drug delivery. To pass that module: Diagram labels carrier, drug, target.)
What do regulators check?
Size distribution, stability and safety. (Covered in module 4: Materials in the body. To pass that module: Table is consistent with sources.)
Name a risk.
Inflammation, accumulation or allergy. (Covered in module 5: Testing and regulation. To pass that module: All stages shown.)
Name a worker control.
Closed systems or masks. (Covered in module 6: Risks and unknowns. To pass that module: Each risk has a control.)
How judge a headline?
Find the evidence stage. (Covered in module 7: Hype and claims. To pass that module: Stage is named for each.)
Who gets access?
A fairness question to state. (Covered in module 8: Write the briefing. To pass that module: Reader repeats three limits.)
Is lab result a cure?
No. (Covered in module 8: Write the briefing. To pass that module: Reader repeats three limits.)
Why monitor after approval?
Long-term effects can appear. (Covered in module 8: Write the briefing. To pass that module: Reader repeats three limits.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others

ladder: The nanoscale

L1: learner can say what nano means. Focus module: The nanoscale (Understand, 2 h). A nanometre is one billionth of a metre. Key points: A hair is about 80,000 nm wide; a virus about 100 nm. Materials behave differently at this size. Units: 1 m = 1,000,000,000 nm.

Teach: open with the worked example. Gold looks red when particles are tiny, not yellow. Then set the activity: Make a size chart from hair to atom. Mark against the standard: Orders of magnitude correct. Check at this level: How many nanometres in a metre? Model answer: 1,000,000,000. Show size chart.
Imaging and diagnostics

L2: learner can name medical uses. Focus module: Imaging and diagnostics (Understand, 2 h). Tiny particles can make signals clearer. Key points: Contrast agents and rapid test strips use nanoparticles. Sensors can detect small amounts of a marker. False results still occur; follow-up tests are needed.

Teach: open with the worked example. A rapid test shows a coloured line using gold particles. Then set the activity: Explain a test strip in your own words. Mark against the standard: Peer understands. Check at this level: Name a medical use. Model answer: Imaging, test strips or drug delivery. Use test strip.
Drug delivery

L3: learner can read size charts. Focus module: Drug delivery (Understand, 3 h). Carriers can protect a drug and aim it. Key points: Lipid particles carry some vaccines and drugs. Targeting may reduce side effects. The body can clear or react to carriers.

Teach: open with the worked example. Fat-based particles shield fragile genetic material during delivery. Then set the activity: Draw a delivery diagram. Mark against the standard: Diagram labels carrier, drug, target. Check at this level: Why does size matter in the body? Model answer: It decides where particles go and how they clear. Draw carrier.
Materials in the body

L4: learner can explain delivery and clearance. Focus module: Materials in the body (Analyse, 3 h). Where particles go matters. Key points: Size, shape and surface decide where they travel. Liver and kidneys clear many particles. Long-term effects need study.

Teach: open with the worked example. Particles above a certain size stay in the liver longer. Then set the activity: Make a table of size and body route. Mark against the standard: Table is consistent with sources. Check at this level: What do regulators check? Model answer: Size distribution, stability and safety. Discuss clearance.
Testing and regulation

L5: learner can review claims and regulation. Focus module: Testing and regulation (Evaluate, 3 h). Nanomedicines go through extra checks. Key points: Lab, animal-free methods where possible, human trials, approval. Regulators ask for size distribution, stability and safety. Post-approval monitoring continues.

Teach: open with the worked example. A batch is rejected because particle size varied. Then set the activity: Map the path from lab to patient. Mark against the standard: All stages shown. Check at this level: Name a risk. Model answer: Inflammation, accumulation or allergy. Map approval path.
Hype and claims

L6: learner can coordinate a lab file. Focus module: Hype and claims (Analyse, 2 h). Sort proven from promised. Key points: Check evidence stage: idea, lab, trial, approved. Be careful with "miracle" words. Look for independent reviews.

Teach: open with the worked example. A news story calls a lab result a cure; the learner marks it "lab stage". Then set the activity: Review three headlines. Mark against the standard: Stage is named for each. Check at this level: Name a worker control. Model answer: Closed systems or masks. Cover records.
Write the briefing
L7: learner can audit a briefing. Focus module: Write the briefing (Create, 3 h). Balance benefit, risk and fairness. Key points: Cover access and cost. State what is unknown. Test with a non-expert.

Teach: open with the worked example. The reader can explain why approval takes years. Then set the activity: Finish and test. Mark against the standard: Reader repeats three limits. Check at this level: How judge a headline? Model answer: Find the evidence stage. Peer audit.
